explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves DONE_IN_PROC row-count messages enabled, adding unnecessary network chatter and potentially breaking client code.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF prevents automatic transaction rollback on many run-time errors, risking partially committed or lingering transactions.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders retrieves all columns, increasing I/O and coupling callers to schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) from Sales.Orders without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary, non-deterministic set of rows.
DISTINCT on Sales.Orders.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is the primary key and already guaranteed unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders allows dirty reads, skipped rows, and duplicate rows during concurrent modifications.
Applying YEAR(o.OrderDate) in the WHERE clause makes the predicate non-sargable and prevents an index range seek.
Comparing int column Sales.Orders.CustomerID to nvarchar(20) variable @CustomerIdText causes an implicit conversion that can degrade plan quality.
The predicate @CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID impedes cardinality estimation and often forces a scan instead of a seek on Sales.Orders.
LIKE N'%urgent%' on Sales.Orders.Comments uses a leading wildcard, preventing a standard index seek.
NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices.CustomerID is fragile because any NULL produced by the subquery causes the entire predicate to evaluate to unknown and return zero rows.
Wrapping Sales.Orders.CustomerID in ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) in the WHERE clause prevents an index seek on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
Performing arithmetic in o.OrderID + 0 = @OrderID makes the predicate non-sargable and prevents a direct seek on PK_Sales_Orders.
The inequality predicate o.CustomerID <> 1 on Sales.Orders is poorly selective and typically results in an index or table scan.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and produces the Cartesian product of both tables.
Joining Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines using a comma-separated FROM list with the join condition in WHERE uses obsolete syntax that obscures join intent.
The correlated scalar subquery counting Sales.OrderLines per Sales.Orders.OrderID evaluates per outer row instead of using a set-based join or aggregation.
The correlated EXISTS subquery against Sales.OrderLines filters Sales.Orders per outer row where a set-based join could be evaluated.
The CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END expression is duplicated in both the SELECT list and the ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 relies on select-list column position, which can silently change sort behavior if columns are reordered or added.
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY orders only by non-unique Sales.Orders.OrderDate without a unique tie-breaker such as OrderID.
UNION between disjoint predicates o.OrderID = 1 and o.OrderID = 2 performs unnecessary duplicate elimination where UNION ALL suffices.
Using (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts every matching row when an EXISTS check would short-circuit on the first match.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders silently accepts multiple rows and leaves @OrderID with an arbitrary last value.
Table variable @OrderIds lacks column statistics and can receive poor cardinality estimates during query optimization.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders implicitly defines the temporary table schema from the query instead of declaring it explicitly.
Cursor order_cursor processes rows from Sales.Orders iteratively instead of using a set-based operation.
The WHILE @Counter <= 1 loop performs iterative row-by-row control flow instead of set-based processing.
Concatenating @CustomerID directly into @Sql prevents plan reuse and introduces dynamic SQL fragility.
EXEC sys.sp_executesql @Sql executes dynamic SQL without parameterized inputs, defeating plan caching and parameter safety.
Temporary table #Scratch is explicitly created with CREATE TABLE but never dropped before the procedure ends.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing via THROW or returning an error status, hiding failures from callers.
RAISERROR is used instead of THROW for raising an error when @OrderID < 0.
PRINT outputs buffered diagnostic text that is unsuitable for structured logging or production procedures.
Filtering Sales.Orders.CustomerID = 1 embeds a hard-coded business identifier directly in the query.
Comparing Sales.Orders.OrderDate >= '20160101' embeds an unlabelled magic date constant in the query predicate.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits an explicit style code, making month/day interpretation dependent on session DATEFORMAT settings.
Using COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) = COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) in the join predicate prevents index seeks and degrades join optimization.
Self-joining Sales.Orders to itself on OrderID only retrieves o.OrderID, which is already available without a join.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts Sales.Orders by an nvarchar(MAX) LOB column, requiring large memory grants and risking tempdb spills.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines table without a WHERE filter.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 applies a row-level filter after GROUP BY instead of filtering rows earlier in a WHERE clause.
ORDER BY OrderCount is redundant because SELECT COUNT(*) without GROUP BY always returns a single row.
MERGE on Sales.Orders carries known SQL Server concurrency and correctness hazards compared to separate DML statements.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments assigns a column to its existing value, generating unnecessary logging and locks.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 deletes using a non-key attribute predicate rather than a stable key.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks the executing worker thread and holds session resources unnecessarily.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is started outside a TRY...CATCH block, risking unhandled errors leaving an open transaction.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON mutates session state and couples application logic to manual identity management.
EXEC sp_who invokes a procedure without an explicit schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 changes a session setting and never resets it to 0, affecting subsequent statements.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) omits an explicit column list, making it fragile to column order or schema changes.
INSERT INTO #DemoCustomers SELECT ... omits an explicit target column list, risking mismatches if table columns change.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' begins with a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
User-supplied parameter @CustomerName is concatenated directly into dynamic SQL string @sql, creating a SQL injection vulnerability.
EXEC sp_executesql @sql runs dynamic SQL without passing parameter definitions or values.
sp_executesql is invoked without the sys schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 lacks a WHERE clause and unconditionally overwrites every row in the table.
Filtering on LEFT JOIN table column o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' in the WHERE clause eliminates NULL-extended rows and turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
Comparing o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' embeds an unlabelled date literal directly in the predicate.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL uses equality against NULL, which evaluates to unknown under ANSI_NULLS ON instead of using IS NULL.
Calling scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list forces row-by-row evaluation across Sales.Customers and can inhibit parallelism.
The CATCH block handles an error raised inside an explicit transaction without rolling back the active transaction.
The CATCH block only runs SELECT ERROR_MESSAGE() and does not rethrow or return an error status, swallowing the failure.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hard-codes a specific index on Sales.Customers, overriding the query optimizer and risking failures or poor plans if indexes change.
Three levels of nested derived tables over Sales.Customers reduce readability and should be flattened or refactored using a CTE.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' uses a leading wildcard on Sales.Customers, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) returns all columns instead of an explicit column list.
Calling multi-statement table-valued function dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti(@CustomerName) prevents query inlining and often causes poor cardinality estimates.
